2.1 Materials

Daily 10km wildfire smoke PM2.5 data, 2006-2023
The wildfire smoke PM2.5 product is produced with a ML method, and the overall R2 is 0.63. Model performance varied spatially, with often very high performance at EPA monitors throughout California, the Pacific Northwest, the upper Midwest, and the Northeast and lower performance at monitors in the Southwest and the South. https://www.stanfordecholab.com/wildfire_smoke.
A smoke PM2.5 prediction of 0 in this file means that the grid cell-day did have a smoke day but did not have elevated PM2.5.
Drought data
Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) data will be used to measure the drought level. The SPEI data cover the contiguous U.S. from 1979 to the present at the spatial resolution of 4 km and are updated monthly. This drought index considers precipitation and potential evapotranspiration to indicate the spatial and temporal extents of drought conditions. The SPEI data can be access through x

section: 3.1 Annual temporary variation of smoke PM2.5
text:
3.1 Annual temporary variation of smoke PM2.5
Annual variation in the California-wide spatial mean of seasonal daily smoke PM₂.₅ is shown in Figure 2. Each point averages the valid raster cells for one year and season, retaining zero-smoke cells.








Figure 2: spatial mean of seasonal daily smoke pm2.5 concentrations for summer and fall





California-wide seasonal mean daily wildfire smoke PM₂.₅ concentrations were generally low before 2016, except for a summer peak in 2008 that coincided with widespread lightning-triggered fires.
Variability increased during 2017-2021, with the highest fall concentration in 2020 (15.70 µg/m³) and the highest summer concentration in 2021 (10.64 µg/m³). These peaks coincided with major wildfire activity, including the August Complex and Creek fires in 2020 and the Dixie and Caldor fires in 2021. Drought, extreme heat, and reduced snowpack likely helped create conditions favorable for severe wildfire activity in 2021. The Concentrations declined sharply in 2022-2023, highlighting the influence of episodic high-smoke years.

text:
3.2 Annual Spatial mean of smoke PM2.5
Plot the daily mean smoke PM₂.₅ concentrations for summer and fall. Figure 3 Mean daily wildfire smoke PM₂.₅ concentrations showed distinct seasonal spatial patterns. In summer, higher concentrations were more widespread across northern California, with the strongest hotspot in the northern interior. In fall, elevated concentrations were more localized, with prominent hotspots in northern and central-eastern California. Coastal areas and much of southern California generally had lower concentrations in both seasons.








Figure 3: California-wide spatial mean of seasonal daily wildfire smoke \(\mathrm{PM}_{2.5}\) concentrations for summer and fall, 2006–2023.

3.3 Seasonal Trend of smoke PM2.5
Calculate pixel-level Sen’s slopes and Mann–Kendall (MK) statistics for summer and fall.


Show Code
library(terra)
library(trend)
library(Kendall)

calc_sen <- function(x) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  if (length(x) < 10) return(NA_real_)
  if (length(unique(x)) == 1) return(0)
  unname(trend::sens.slope(x)$estimates)}

calc_mk <- function(x) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  if (length(x) < 10) return(NA_real_)
  if (length(unique(x)) == 1) return(NA_real_)
  unname(Kendall::MannKendall(x)$sl)}

# Calculate Sen's slope
summer_sen <- app(summer, fun = calc_sen)
fall_sen   <- app(fall, fun = calc_sen)
# Calculate Mann-Kendall p-values
summer_mk <- app(summer, fun = calc_mk)
fall_mk   <- app(fall, fun = calc_mk)

# Combine slope and p-value into two bands.
summer_result <- c(summer_sen, summer_mk)
fall_result <- c(fall_sen, fall_mk)
names(summer_result) <- c("Sen_slope", "MK_pvalue")
names(fall_result) <- c("Sen_slope", "MK_pvalue")

# Save one two-band GeoTIFF per season.
